The client wants https://api.notes.example/notes/42. The hostname api.notes.example names the destination. DNS discovers an address for that name. It does not resolve the path /notes/42. Relevant caches start empty, so this lookup cannot reuse a stored answer.

The stub resolver is the client's local lookup helper. It asks a recursive resolver to obtain the answer. The stub does not itself walk the hierarchy. An authoritative server answers from the records it serves for a zone, a managed portion of the DNS name space. Delegation assigns a child zone to its authoritative servers. A referral points the resolver at those servers. A referral is not the final host address.

The recursive resolver asks the root and receives a referral to .example. It asks that .example authority and follows its referral to the notes.example authority. Root does not hold every host address. The notes.example authority holds the final records for api.notes.example. Those records include a CNAME: api.notes.example is an alias for the DNS name edge.notes.example, not an IP address, URL, or HTTP path. The alias does not redirect /notes/42. Resolution follows the target to obtain address data. An A record supplies an IPv4 address. An AAAA record supplies an IPv6 address. The client uses an address family it can reach. The target's A or AAAA data may already be returned with the alias; otherwise a further lookup is required. Without usable target address data, the alias alone gives the client nothing to connect to. The alias also adds a dependency on the target's DNS data even if one team manages both names. The recursive resolver returns the resulting address to the stub.

The client then connects to that address and sends the HTTPS request for /notes/42. That request and its response do not pass through the DNS servers. An address answer does not prove that Notes is healthy or able to serve the note.

Later, a usable cached address or an existing connection can avoid a fresh lookup. Cached answers can skip authority visits, and cached delegations can let the resolver start closer to the answer. The alias and the target address records can be cached separately.

evidence.quote: A hostname, api.notes.example, names a network destination. An IP address is the network address used to reach it.

DNS, the Domain Name System, provides name discovery. A DNS record is typed data associated with a name. For this web lookup, the client obtains address records, connects to an address, and sends the HTTPS request for /notes/42.

DNS resolves the hostname, not the HTTP path. The later note request and response do not pass through the DNS servers. An address answer does not prove the Notes API is healthy or able to serve that note.
A cache temporarily reuses a stored answer. A usable cached address or an existing connection can avoid a fresh lookup for the next request.

The stub resolver is the client's local lookup helper. It asks a recursive resolver to obtain an answer on its behalf. An authoritative server answers from the records it serves for a zone, a managed portion of DNS names.
Delegation assigns responsibility for a child zone to its authoritative servers. A referral points the resolver toward those servers; it is not the final host address.

The recursive resolver asks root, receives a referral to .example, asks that authority, then follows its referral to the notes.example authority. That authority holds the final records for api.notes.example. Root does not hold every host's address.

The recursive resolver returns the result to the stub. Cached answers can avoid the authority visits; cached delegations can let the resolver start closer to the answer. The stub need not perform each visit itself.
An A record supplies an IPv4 address, such as 192.0.2.10. An AAAA record supplies an IPv6 address, such as 2001:db8::10. A client uses an address family it can reach.

A CNAME record is a name alias. If api.notes.example points to edge.notes.example, resolution follows that target name to obtain its A or AAAA data. The needed data may already be cached or returned with the alias; otherwise further lookup is needed.

The alias contains a DNS name, not an IP address, URL or HTTP path. It does not redirect /notes/42. Without usable target address data, the alias alone cannot give the client an address to connect to.
Alias and target records can be cached separately. The alias adds a dependency on the target's DNS data, even if both names are managed by the same team.

TTL, time to live, limits ordinary cache reuse in seconds. Each cache ages the TTL it received with that answer. It is not a worldwide update timer, and a new TTL cannot rewrite an old cached answer.

This resolver cached the old address at 11:59 with the 3600-second TTL it received then. At noon the record's TTL is lowered to 60 seconds and the address is changed. That edit does not rewrite the entry already cached. The same rule as a resolver that cached a 300-second TTL at 10:00 and could keep using it until 10:05 after a 10:01 edit applies here: the existing entry stays ordinarily usable until the TTL it received runs out, 3600 seconds after 11:59, not by 12:01. The resolver need not refresh by 12:01.

A safer planned change lowers the TTL first, to 60 seconds, then waits until the previous 3600-second TTL has aged out, and only then switches the address. Keep the old destination usable through that overlap. Monitor traffic, errors, and existing connections at both destinations. DNS edits do not move open connections.

Short TTLs cost more refresh queries and make clients depend on working DNS more often. TTL is not a worldwide cutover. Independent caches and connection lifetimes prevent everyone from switching at once. Some resolvers can still serve expired data when a refresh fails, so TTL is not a hard global recovery deadline.

evidence.quote: A new TTL cannot rewrite an old cached answer
TTL, or time to live, limits ordinary cache reuse in seconds. Each cache ages the TTL it received; it is not a worldwide update timer.

A resolver caches the old address at 10:00 with a 300-second TTL. At 10:01 we change the address and lower TTL to 30 seconds. Its existing entry can still be ordinarily usable until 10:05; the edit does not rewrite that entry.

For a planned move, lower TTL first, allow the previous longer TTL to age out, then switch. Keep the old destination usable through the transition while monitoring traffic, errors and existing connections at both destinations. DNS edits do not migrate open connections.

Shorter TTLs mean more refresh queries and more frequent dependence on working DNS. Independent caches and connection lifetimes prevent a simultaneous cutover. Some resolvers can even serve expired data when refreshing fails, so TTL is not a hard global recovery deadline.
Plan overlap and observe clients; a TTL edit is not a cache purge.

Negative caching reuses an answer that reports absence. Before the name existed, this resolver cached NXDOMAIN for api.notes.example. NXDOMAIN says the queried name does not exist. Adding the name and a 30-second A record does not notify that cache. The negative answer has its own cache lifetime. The new positive record's TTL does not clear it, so the resolver can keep reporting absence until that negative lifetime ends.

NODATA is a different absence answer. The name exists, but it has no record of the requested type. A response with no AAAA record does not mean there is no A record, and it does not mean the name is missing.

SERVFAIL means resolution could not be completed, for example because the resolver could not obtain a usable answer. It is not proof that the name does not exist. Resolution failures may also be cached, so a failure can be reused to avoid hammering failing DNS servers.

Check the name, the record type, and the status before changing records. A cached NXDOMAIN, a missing type, and a lookup failure are different problems.

evidence.quote: Negative caching reuses an answer reporting absence. NXDOMAIN says the queried name does not exist. NODATA means the name exists but has no record of the requested type: no AAAA record does not imply no A record or no name.

Suppose a resolver cached NXDOMAIN before we created api.notes.example. Adding its A record does not notify that cache. The negative answer has its own cache lifetime; the new positive record's TTL does not clear it.

SERVFAIL means resolution could not be completed, for example because the resolver could not obtain usable answers. It is not proof that the name does not exist. Resolution failures may also be cached to avoid repeatedly hammering failing DNS servers.
Check the requested name, record type and returned status before changing records. A missing type, a cached absent name and a lookup failure call for different investigations.
Distinguish an answer about absence from a failure to obtain an answer.

Steering is DNS selecting the destinations it returns in answers. Failover changes that selected destination after a failure. Ordinary DNS records do not detect that east's application is unhealthy. A separate health check and policy, or an operator, must notice east's failure and change the answers so new lookups return west.

Returning each endpoint for some lookups does not put half of the HTTP requests on each endpoint. A shared recursive resolver can reuse one answer for many clients, and each client can send many requests on that address or connection. Equal DNS answers are not an equal split of requests.

Removing east from new answers does not instantly move everyone. Clients with the old answer cached can still try east until that cache entry stops being reused. Existing connections do not migrate to west just because DNS changed. DNS is not choosing a destination again for every HTTP request.

For recovery, west must be reachable and healthy and must have enough spare capacity for the redirected work. A health signal is only a sample. It does not promise every request succeeds. Changing DNS does not create that capacity and does not guarantee instant recovery.

evidence.quote: DNS traffic steering selects destinations returned in answers. Failover changes the selected destination after failure. For Notes east and west, a separate health check and policy, or an operator, must detect east's failure and change answers. Ordinary DNS records do not detect application health themselves.

Returning east for half of lookups does not guarantee half of HTTP requests reach east. A shared recursive resolver can reuse one answer for many clients, and each client may send many requests using that address or connection.

After east is removed from new answers, cached clients can still try it. Existing connections do not migrate to west just because DNS changed. DNS is not choosing a destination again for every HTTP request.

West must be reachable, healthy and have enough spare capacity for redirected work. A health signal is a sample, not a promise that every request succeeds; DNS changes do not create capacity or guarantee instant recovery.
DNS steers future address discovery, subject to caches and client behavior.

These outcomes come from different steps. A client that already has a usable cached address can still connect during a DNS problem, and an open connection can keep working with no new lookup. That is why some users with open sessions still work. New users who need a fresh lookup cannot resolve api.notes.example when the recursive resolver, the delegation, or the authoritative servers cannot answer.

The user who gets the expected address and then an HTTP 500 has finished name discovery. HTTP 500 means the HTTP service responded with an error. It is not, by itself, a DNS lookup failure. Successful DNS does not prove the application works. After the expected address is obtained, inspect the connection, HTTPS, and the application separately.

To separate the failures, start at the client's recursive resolver. Inspect the queried name and type, the answer or error, and the remaining TTL. If the result is wrong or failing, compare the authoritative data and the parent delegation. An authoritative new address next to a cached old one is a cache-age question, not an automatic reason to edit the record again. A resolver or delegation problem shows up as a lookup error or a wrong or stale answer. A connection, certificate, or application problem shows up only after an address was obtained.

Reachable alternate resolvers and authoritative servers reduce the loss of one DNS server. They do not fix a shared wrong record, a broken delegation, or a failed Notes API. Several DNS servers with the same bad configuration can all return that same wrong result.

evidence.quote: During a DNS outage, a client with a usable cached address may still connect, and an open connection may keep working without a lookup. Fresh uncached lookups need a reachable recursive resolver, working delegation and authoritative servers that can answer.

Reachable alternate resolvers and authoritative servers reduce individual server failures. They cannot fix a shared wrong record, broken delegation or a failed Notes API. Several DNS servers with the same bad configuration can return the same wrong result.

Start with the client's recursive resolver: inspect the queried name and type, its answer or error, and remaining TTL. Compare authoritative data and parent delegation when results are wrong or failing. An authoritative new address beside a cached old one suggests a cache-age question, not an automatic need for another edit.

Once the expected address is obtained, inspect connection, HTTPS and application results separately. HTTP 500 means an HTTP service responded with an error; it is not by itself a DNS lookup failure. Successful DNS does not prove the application works.
Locate the failed step before changing DNS or the application.

DNSSEC adds signatures to DNS data. A validating resolver checks those signatures through a chain of trust: each trusted signing key vouches for the next link, starting from a configured trusted key. Successful validation establishes the origin and integrity of the signed DNS data. It means the data was not altered without detection.

That validates DNS data, not the Notes application. It does not hide the query: DNSSEC does not encrypt the query. It does not prove Notes is healthy, and it does not guarantee availability. It does not remove the HTTPS certificate check. Unsigned data also does not get these signature checks just because the resolver supports DNSSEC.

HTTPS separately authenticates the endpoint by certificate validation and encrypts the HTTP exchange. The client must still verify the certificate for the hostname it requested, api.notes.example, even if DNS followed an alias to another name. A valid DNSSEC answer does not replace that check. Reaching a real server also does not grant permission to read every note. The application's access rules still apply.

evidence.quote: DNSSEC adds signatures to DNS data. A validating resolver checks those signatures through a chain of trust: each trusted signing key vouches for the next link, starting at a configured trusted key. Successful validation establishes the signed data's origin and integrity, meaning it has not been altered without detection.

That validates DNS data, not the Notes application. DNSSEC does not encrypt the query, certify service health or guarantee availability. Unsigned data does not gain these signature checks merely because a resolver supports DNSSEC.

HTTPS separately authenticates the endpoint through certificate validation and encrypts the HTTP exchange. The client must still verify the certificate for the hostname it requested, api.notes.example, even if DNS followed an alias to edge.notes.example.
A valid DNSSEC answer does not remove HTTPS certificate checks. Nor does discovering a real server give the caller permission to read every note; the application's access rules still apply.
DNSSEC protects DNS data; HTTPS protects the connection to the requested service identity.
